title: The 1960s in Color: Life in Small-Town America

scenes.text: Most of us remember the early sixties in black and white. The old photographs in the family album. The news footage. The television shows. But that's not how it looked. The sky was blue. The cars were turquoise and coral and cream. The aprons had yellow flowers on them. Today, let's see it the way it really was. In color.
scenes.caption: IN FULL COLOR

scenes.text: We're going to walk through one small American town, from one end to the other, in the early nineteen sixties. The main street. The diner. The school. The church. The barber shop. The houses with the porch lights on at dusk. If you grew up in a town like this, you're about to go home.
scenes.caption: ONE SMALL TOWN

scenes.text: This town could be in Ohio, or Kansas, or North Carolina, or upstate New York. In nineteen sixty-two, about thirty percent of Americans lived in places with fewer than twenty-five hundred people, and millions more in towns not much bigger. They all looked a little different. And somehow, they all looked exactly the same.
scenes.caption: SOMEWHERE IN AMERICA

scenes.text: Main Street was the heart of everything. On one block you'd find the bank, the hardware store, the five-and-dime, the drugstore, the shoe store, the movie theater, and a department store with mannequins in the windows. Every building had a name painted on the brick, and every name belonged to a family in town.
scenes.caption: THE HEART OF TOWN

scenes.text: Saturday was the big day. Farm families drove in from the countryside to shop. The sidewalks filled up. Mothers went from store to store with lists in their purses, while fathers stood outside the hardware store talking about the weather, the crops and the ball game.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY IN TOWN

scenes.text: The five-and-dime was where kids spent their allowances. Candy by the pound from glass cases. Comic books for twelve cents. Toy cap guns, jacks, marbles, model airplane kits, and goldfish in a tank at the back. The wooden floors creaked under your feet, and the whole store smelled of popcorn and floor polish.
scenes.caption: THE FIVE-AND-DIME

scenes.text: At the drugstore, the soda fountain was still open. You sat on a spinning stool at the marble counter, and the soda jerk made you a cherry phosphate or a chocolate malt in a tall glass. The pharmacist knew every family's prescriptions by heart, and he'd often deliver them himself on the way home.
scenes.caption: THE SODA FOUNTAIN

scenes.text: Parking was diagonal, right in front of the stores, and a nickel in the meter bought an hour. The cars along the curb were a parade of color. Two-tone Chevrolets in turquoise and white. Pink Cadillacs. Station wagons with fake wood on the sides. Pickup trucks, dusty from the farm roads.
scenes.caption: A PARADE OF COLOR

scenes.text: Above the stores, on the second floor, were the offices. The doctor. The dentist. The lawyer. The insurance man. You climbed a narrow staircase with a brass railing and a door with gold letters painted on frosted glass. The dentist's drill could be heard from the sidewalk on a quiet afternoon.
scenes.caption: UP THE STAIRS

scenes.text: Down the street was the diner, a long room with booths along the windows and a counter with stools. The waitress called everybody honey and refilled your coffee without asking. Breakfast was eggs, bacon, toast and hash browns for well under a dollar. The pie case by the register held lemon meringue, apple and cherry.
scenes.caption: THE DINER
scenes.chapter: The diner and the barber shop

scenes.text: The same men sat at the same stools every morning. Farmers, mail carriers, the police chief, the man who owned the feed store. They knew everything that happened in town before the newspaper did. If you wanted to know who was sick, who was courting, or whose barn burned down, you went to the diner.
scenes.caption: THE MORNING REGULARS

scenes.text: Next door was the barber shop, with its red, white and blue pole turning slowly outside. Inside, three chairs, a row of men waiting, a stack of magazines, and a radio tuned to the ball game. A haircut cost around a dollar and a half. Little boys sat on a board laid across the arms of the chair.
scenes.caption: THE BARBER POLE

scenes.text: Most boys got the same haircut. Short on the sides, a little longer on top, maybe a flat-top held up with a pink stick of wax. Nobody asked what style you wanted. The barber looked at you, looked at your father, and went to work. And afterward, he handed you a lollipop.
scenes.caption: THE FLAT-TOP

scenes.text: Across from the barber was the post office, with its flag out front and its brass mailboxes inside, each with a little window and a combination dial. The postmaster knew every family in town by name, and often by handwriting. Letters from sons in the army were handed across the counter with a smile and a question about how he was doing.
scenes.caption: THE POST OFFICE

scenes.text: At the edge of town stood the school, often a big brick building with tall windows and the year it was built carved over the door. In smaller towns, all twelve grades might be under one roof. The same teachers taught the children of the children they had taught twenty years before.
scenes.caption: THE BRICK SCHOOL

scenes.text: The classrooms had wooden desks with inkwell holes nobody used anymore, a clock on the wall that ticked loudly in the afternoons, and a portrait of George Washington above the blackboard. Every morning began with the Pledge of Allegiance, hands over hearts, facing the flag in the corner.
scenes.caption: THE PLEDGE

scenes.text: At lunch, the cafeteria served food on divided trays. Sloppy joes, fish sticks on Friday, a square of yellow cake with chocolate frosting. Milk came in small glass bottles or the new little cardboard cartons. At recess, the girls jumped rope and the boys played baseball on a dusty field behind the building.
scenes.caption: THE CAFETERIA

scenes.text: After school, the big yellow buses lined up out front. Town kids walked home, stopping at the drugstore on the way. Farm kids rode the bus for an hour, past the grain elevator and the water tower, and then went straight to chores, feeding the animals before supper.
scenes.caption: THE RIDE HOME

scenes.text: Friday nights in the fall belonged to the high school football team. The whole town turned out under the lights. The band marched at halftime in uniforms with gold braid. The cheerleaders wore saddle shoes and pleated skirts. And on Monday morning, the game was all anybody talked about at the diner.
scenes.caption: FRIDAY NIGHT

scenes.text: The houses in town sat on wide lots with big shade trees. White frame houses with green shutters. Brick bungalows with front porches. Newer ranch houses on the edge of town, in pale yellow or mint green, each with a picture window and a carport. Nobody locked the front door, and the keys stayed in the car.
scenes.caption: NOBODY LOCKED THE DOOR

scenes.text: The porch was where life happened in the evening. You sat in a glider or on the steps after supper, and people walking by stopped to talk. The radio played softly through the screen door. Fireflies came out over the lawn. And down the street, a mother called her children home.
scenes.caption: THE FRONT PORCH

scenes.text: Inside, the kitchens were full of color too. Pink or turquoise appliances. Yellow Formica countertops. A chrome dinette set with red vinyl chairs. Curtains with roosters or teapots printed on them. A clock shaped like a sunburst. Women's magazines told homemakers that color made a happy home, and they believed it.
scenes.caption: A PINK KITCHEN

scenes.text: Monday was wash day all over town. Sheets and shirts flapped on clotheslines in every backyard, and the women talked over the fences while they hung them up. A lot of families now owned an electric washing machine, but almost everybody still dried the laundry outside in the sun and wind.
scenes.caption: WASH DAY

scenes.text: Out back there was a garden, a swing set made of pipes, and maybe a barbecue grill made of bricks that a father had built himself. On summer weekends, the smell of charcoal and hamburgers drifted over every fence. Neighbors came by with a dish of potato salad and stayed until dark.
scenes.caption: THE BACKYARD GRILL

scenes.text: On Sunday morning, the church bells rang all over town. Families walked or drove to church in their best clothes. The women wore hats and gloves. The little girls wore patent leather shoes that pinched. The little boys wore clip-on ties and tried not to fidget during the sermon.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY BEST

scenes.text: After church came Sunday dinner, the biggest meal of the week, often in the middle of the day. Roast beef or fried chicken, mashed potatoes, green beans from the garden, homemade rolls, and pie. Grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins crowded around the table, and the children ate in the kitchen.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY DINNER

scenes.text: In the summer, the whole town went to the municipal swimming pool, which opened on Memorial Day and closed on Labor Day. The water smelled of chlorine. The concrete burned your feet. And the high dive was the test of courage for every ten-year-old in town.
scenes.caption: THE TOWN POOL

scenes.text: On summer evenings there was Little League at the ball field, with the parents in the bleachers and the coach chewing on a toothpick. On the Fourth of July there was a parade down Main Street, a picnic in the park, and fireworks over the water tower. Everybody came. Everybody.
scenes.query: 1960s parade small town Fourth of July
scenes.caption: THE FOURTH OF JULY

scenes.text: And in the late summer came the county fair. Prize pigs, prize pies and prize quilts. A Ferris wheel and a merry-go-round. Cotton candy, caramel apples and corn dogs. Teenagers walked the midway holding hands for the first time. For a lot of kids, it was the best week of the whole year.
scenes.caption: THE COUNTY FAIR

scenes.text: And on the edge of town, there was always the drive-in theater. A giant white screen standing alone in a field. A speaker that hung on your car window. Children in pajamas in the back seat, asleep before the second feature. A carload of teenagers, one or two of them hiding in the trunk to save the price of admission.
scenes.caption: THE DRIVE-IN

scenes.text: As the sun went down, the neon signs came on along Main Street. The red letters over the movie theater. The green glow of the drugstore sign. The theater marquee announced the Saturday picture, and teenagers lined up outside with their dates, pretending not to be nervous.
scenes.caption: WHEN THE NEON CAME ON

scenes.text: Teenagers cruised the main street in their fathers' cars, turning around in the parking lot of the drive-in at one end and the gas station at the other. Back and forth. Back and forth. The radios were tuned to the same station, so the same song seemed to be playing from every car at once.
scenes.caption: BACK AND FORTH

scenes.text: By ten o'clock, most of the town was dark. The stores were closed. A police car drove slowly down Main Street, the officer checking that the shop doors were locked. And in the houses along the quiet streets, the television played the late news, and then the national anthem, and then the snow.
scenes.caption: THE QUIET STREETS

scenes.text: Those small towns are still out there. But many of the stores on Main Street are empty now, and the diner closed years ago, and the movie theater became a church or an antique shop. The kids who rode their bicycles to the five-and-dime grew up, and a lot of them moved away.
scenes.caption: STILL OUT THERE

scenes.text: Maybe that's why those old color pictures hit so hard. In black and white, the past looks like history. In color, it looks like a place you could walk back into. The turquoise car. Your mother's yellow apron. The red stools at the soda fountain. It was real. And it was yours.
scenes.caption: A PLACE YOU COULD WALK BACK INTO

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was the name of your hometown, and what was on its main street? We read every comment. And stay with us, because next we're going to put nineteen sixty-two side by side with today, and ask who really had it better. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR HOMETOWN?
